bill_description: H.R.28 is a bill in the U.S. House of Representatives. This review uses the version the House passed on January 14, 2025. The bill would change Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in schools and colleges that receive federal money. Those schools could not let a person the bill classifies as male take part in a sports program for women or girls. The bill would decide sex “based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” It would still allow males to train or practice with those teams if no female loses a team place, a chance to play, a scholarship, admission to a school or another sports benefit. It also orders a federal study of benefits that girls could lose. Each argument compares the bill with the law in force on January 14, 2025.

claims.title: The sports rule and its definition of sex
claims.statement: This rule covers a school or college that receives federal money and runs, sponsors or facilitates sports. It may not let a person whose sex is male, as the bill defines it, take part in a sports program designated for women or girls. The bill defines sex for this rule based only on reproductive biology and genetics at birth.

claims.title: The law in force on January 14, 2025
claims.statement: On January 14, 2025, federal law had no express rule on transgender athletes. Some schools, states and sports organizations let transgender girls and women compete in girls’ and women’s sports, with or without conditions. Others did not.
claims.classification_reason: Adequately sourced by Congress’s research office and the sports rules themselves, and no response challenges it. It sets the comparison; it is not a vote and does not show that any change is good or bad.
claims.scope_html: Practice differed by place. The bill would change the rule only where this participation was allowed. Later events, such as the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) rule change on February 6, 2025, are not part of this comparison.
claims.background_html: The Congressional Research Service (CRS) is Congress’s research office. The report quoted here was updated in August 2025. Regulations are rules written by a government agency. The NCAA is the main college sports organization.
claims.support_html:
CRS says: “Neither the statute nor the regulations currently address how Title IX applies to transgender athletes.” [1] The 2024 Title IX regulations were already canceled, because “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [1] Older rules allowed separate teams: “Long-standing Title IX regulations permit separation of the sexes in school sports programs provided schools offer equal athletic opportunities.” [2]

CRS also says some places let transgender students compete “with no particular requirements or restrictions.” [3] College sports used limits on testosterone, a hormone: “Between January 19, 2022, and February 6, 2025, the NCAA called for the participation of transgender athletes to be regulated on a sport-by-sport basis.” [4] Elsewhere, states had laws “requiring student-athletes to participate on teams according to their sex assigned at birth.” [3]

claims.title: Physical mismatch in women’s contact sports
claims.statement: In women’s contact competition, such as rugby, athletes who went through male puberty can keep differences in size, speed and force after lowering testosterone. These differences can raise the risk of collision injury for smaller players.
claims.classification_reason: This modest collision-risk proposition has no retained response disputing it. Modeling limits, international scope and low-certainty fitness evidence remain visible qualifications; they do not require an extra shared vote about a possibility.
claims.scope_html: This claim covers contact competition only. It does not cover athletes who did not go through male puberty. The evidence is not a measured count of injuries involving transgender players. World Rugby’s conclusion was for “the international level of the game” [1], and its guidance does “not preclude national unions from flexibility in their application of the guidelines at the domestic/community level of the game” [1]. Rejecting this claim does not reject other routes in an argument.
claims.background_html: World Rugby is the international body for rugby, a sport with frequent physical contact. Testosterone is a hormone. A tackle is when one player stops another by force.
claims.support_html:
World Rugby says: “Forces and inertia faced by a smaller and slower player during frequent collisions are significantly greater when in contact with a much larger, faster player.” [2] It adds that “large discrepancies create greater risks for smaller and slower players” [3]. It concludes that “this comparatively small effect of testosterone reduction allows substantial and meaningful differences to remain.” [2]

The limits are also in the sources. World Rugby’s summary says: “To date, no direct studies on trans women rugby players.” [4] A 2026 review reports “higher lean mass” [5] in transgender women but says “their physical fitness was comparable.” [5] It calls the evidence “mostly low certainty” [5].

prerequisite_paths.reason: The mismatch matters here only because the bill’s rule would remove these matchups from covered competition.

claims.title: Invasive bodily checks
claims.statement: H.R.28 sets a biological test and no method for checking it. Because of this, schools would come under pressure to use invasive bodily checks. Those checks would expose girls to humiliation, distress or sexual abuse.
claims.classification_reason: Substantive objection repeated in four responses: the text adds no examination procedure, Idaho’s exams came from a separate statute, and most comparable states used birth certificates.
claims.scope_html: This claim is only about bodily checks. It is not about questions based on records, interviews, public accusations, or fear of being challenged. Rejecting it blocks only the routes that need bodily checks.
claims.background_html: A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs. The Ninth Circuit is a federal appeals court. The Supreme Court’s June 30, 2026 decision reversed that court’s Idaho judgment, which came after the comparison date.
claims.support_html: Representative Hayes says the bill “provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [1]. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn of “a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2] and say: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2]. A federal appeals court described Idaho’s law as allowing checks “including gynecological exams.” [3] The bill’s test remains “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [4]
claims.objection_html: The bill’s text sets no examination procedure. arguments.title: It protects women’s fair chance to earn sports wins and recognition.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 It protects women’s fair chance to earn sports wins and recognition.

  • Because Male puberty builds strength. Testosterone is a hormone, and a review of research explains that “increases in testosterone due to puberty promote muscular strength” [5].
  • Because The review looked at 24 studies of transgender women who were not athletes. Here, transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women. After 12 to 36 months of hormone treatment, the review said: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5] Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.
  • Because Strength matters in speed and power events: “In sports demanding speed and power, muscular strength and the ability to generate high rates of force are recognised as key determinant in athletic success.” [5]
  • So In events that depend on strength, the bill would keep strength advantages retained from male puberty out of the female category. Giving women a real chance to earn sports rewards serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunity and just treatment.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not settle whether transgender women who train and compete keep the speed and power advantage this fairness argument needs.

  • Because The review says the effects on people who train are not known. GAHT means hormone treatment that matches gender identity: “the effects of GAHT on these parameters, or indeed athletic performance in transgender people who engage in training and competition, remain unknown.” [5]
  • Because The review does not say whether the compared groups trained the same amount: “The levels of physical activity of the transwomen compared with cisgender women in the studies were not reported.” [5]
  • Because A 2024 study measured athletes at one point in time and found mixed results. Compared with cisgender women athletes, transgender women athletes had “higher absolute handgrip strength” [6] but “lower relative jump height” [6]. Relative jump height takes body weight into account.
  • So Strength kept by people who are not athletes does not show an advantage among trained athletes in a speed or power event. The one athlete study points in both directions. Its authors write: “Sports-specific studies are necessary to inform policy-making.” [6] This response does not show that no advantage exists. It also does not address places without hormone limits.

arguments.title: It protects girls’ places in sports and their chances to gain education, health and leadership benefits.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects girls’ places in sports and their chances to gain education, health and leadership benefits.

  • Because Former college swimmer Paula Scanlan told a House committee that places were actually lost: “I know women who have lost roster spots and spots on the podium.” [10] A roster spot is a place on a team. A podium spot is a top finish in a race.
  • Because The bill allows male training or practice only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where places or sports money are limited, the competition ban and the practice condition protect female athletes from losing them to male participants. For a girl who needs sports money to attend college, protecting that money keeps open a way into education.
  • Because Girls in positive sports programs report better mental health. A 2024 study found: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]
  • Because A 2024 survey of U.S. adults who had played girls’ or women’s sports found reported gains in leadership skills: “Half of women (48.6%) credit the skills acquired through sports for their leadership development.” [12]
  • So Keeping a girl’s place in a good program keeps her chance to gain these benefits. Protecting these ways into education, well-being and adult leadership serves [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities in life.
arguments.con_html:
Response Protecting a place does not by itself show that opportunity has become more equal. This reason depends on the fairness claim in Point 1.

  • Because The bill’s practice exception requires that “no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • So Where a place is limited, the bill decides which student holds it. That shows who keeps the benefit. It does not show that this division of places is fairer.
  • Because The mental-health finding is about access to a good program: “Girls who play sport in positive environments report significantly lower levels of anxiety and depression than those who previously played or never played.” [11]

arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 It takes away a route to learning and educational opportunities that other students keep.

  • Because Sports teach useful skills: “Sports provide meaningful opportunities for kids to feel confident in themselves and learn valuable life lessons about teamwork, leadership, and communication.” [2]
  • Because Being on a team also brings educational chances. The bill itself names “scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the athletic program or activity.” [1]
  • Because The ban reaches beyond games to “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Conditional upon participation means open only to people on the team.
  • Because The same birth-based rule also restricts nonbinary students it classifies as male. Nonbinary students do not identify only as girls or boys. The Congressional Equality Caucus, a group of members of Congress, explains: “It would also limit the ability of non-binary and intersex students to participate in these programs as well.” [20]
  • Because Girls born with variations in sex traits, called intersex variations, also face uncertain eligibility. The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn: “There is no principled way to apply the bill's unclear language to the many girls and young women born with intersex variations” [2]. They describe the result: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [2]
  • So Blocking team competition and the activities tied to it takes away chances to learn and advance. [NAME]’s concern for equal opportunities includes transgender, nonbinary and intersex students, which gives a reason to oppose these barriers.
  • Note Permission for “males to train or practice” [1] gives back neither eligibility to compete nor equal access to team places and benefits. Even practice is conditional: it is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport” [1], among other protected opportunities.
arguments.con_html:
Response For students who have gone through male puberty, listing the benefits of a lost team place does not show that the eligibility rule denies equal opportunity.

  • Because Fair opportunity can require limits on who enters a sports category. In the Clark case, a court upheld keeping boys off a girls’ volleyball team because “due to average physiological differences, males would displace females to a substantial extent if they were allowed to compete for positions on the volleyball team.” [21] The reason was a real difference affecting fair competition, not just that separate teams exist.
  • Because Having been eligible under a testosterone limit does not show equal competitive conditions. Reviewing physical traits after male puberty, researchers Hilton and Lundberg reported that “the muscular advantage enjoyed by transgender women is only minimally reduced when testosterone is suppressed.” [22]
  • So Equal opportunity requires a fair basis for eligibility, not keeping every existing route to scholarships, learning or admission. For these students, the argument must show why this boundary unfairly blocks comparable students. Naming benefits and affected identities does not supply that step.
  • Note This response depends on the disputed claim that an advantage remains. A 2026 review reports: “Current evidence is mostly low certainty and has heterogenous quality but does not support theories of inherent athletic advantages for transgender women over cisgender.” [8]
  • So This response does not reach students who have not gone through male puberty, sports where no advantage has been shown, or eligible girls deterred by uncertainty about intersex variations.

arguments.title: Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 5 Enforcing the birth-sex rule puts children’s privacy, dignity and bodily safety at risk.

  • Because Schools must apply the rule without a set way to check it. Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [28]
  • Because A comparable ban in Florida led to questions about a child’s private history. The Associated Press (AP) reported: “They interviewed officials at Monarch and at the daughter's middle and elementary schools, seeking to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29]
  • Because The investigation also asked teammates about her body: “When investigators interviewed the Monarch volleyball players, they said the team did not change clothes or shower together, so they were never disrobed with Norton's daughter.” [29] Disrobed means undressed.
  • Because After the investigation began, the girl left the school. AP reported: “That all ended when the investigation began and the girl left Monarch.” [29] It added: “The girl now attends school online.” [29]
  • Because Women’s rights organizations warn that checking sex may involve “forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [2]. They name a further danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [2].
  • So A nationwide duty to enforce birth-sex eligibility creates grounds for the same kind of intrusive questions, with risks of exposure, humiliation and disrupted schooling and, as those organizations warn, abuse. Protecting children from these harms gives [NAME] a reason to oppose the rule.
  • Note A supporter replies: “There is no requirement for inspections” [2]. That does not answer the risk. The documented records checks and interviews already invaded privacy, and they did not need an exam requirement.
arguments.con_html:
Response The evidence does not establish that the bill would lead to bodily examinations or to sexual abuse resulting from them.

  • Because H.R.28 restricts participation in programs “designated for women or girls.” [1] Its text adds no requirement for bodily examinations.
  • Because AP describes questions about records and knowledge: investigators sought “to find out who knew the girl was transgender and when and how her records were changed.” [29] That account reports no bodily examination.
  • Because Florida’s birth-sex law gives a way to decide eligibility from records: a birth certificate is accepted if its sex statement “was filed at or near the time of the student's birth.” [30]
  • So The step to bodily examinations and sexual abuse rests on an organization’s warning, not on a documented case in this evidence. This response does not answer the documented privacy harms from records checks and interviews, or the disrupted schooling that followed.

NCAA policy already required annual eligibility documentation from transgender women athletes.   • Because The bill makes inclusion a new violation of Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education: “It shall be a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance” [1] to allow the participation it bars.   • Because Existing enforcement law allows “the termination of or refusal to grant or to continue assistance under such program or activity” [36] after an “express finding on the record, after opportunity for hearing, of a failure to comply with such requirement” [36]. It also requires a finding “that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means.” [36] So money can be stopped only after a hearing, a formal finding and a failed attempt to get voluntary compliance.
  • Because That money supports education beyond the individual athlete. The Congressional Research Service (CRS), Congress’s research office, explains: “The Department of Education (ED) distributes substantial funding to elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions” [7].
  • So Schools that keep including these students would put money for the affected program at risk, which could also harm other students. [NAME]’s concern for students’ equal opportunities gives a reason to oppose making inclusion grounds for withdrawing that support.

arguments.title: The bill removes a barrier to playing for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes the bill defines as male.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The bill removes a barrier to playing for girls whose beliefs rule out competing against athletes the bill defines as male.

  • Because This kind of objection has led a team to give up a game: “A Vermont Christian high school forfeited a girls basketball game because the opposing team had a transgender player, the head of school said.” [4] To forfeit means to give up a game.
  • Because The school’s court complaint explains the religious basis of its objection: “sex is immutable.” [5] Immutable means it cannot change. The complaint says that playing that game would affirm the opposite, “in violation of its beliefs.” [5]
  • So In covered girls’ competitions, the bill removes the matchup that causes this objection. Girls with that belief can compete without giving it up.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement includes accepting girls whose religious or other beliefs differ from [NAME]’s. Keeping a way for them to play puts that acceptance into practice.
  • So [NAME] has a reason grounded in tolerance to favor removing this cost of disagreement.
  • Note There is also room to cooperate across the competition rule. The bill allows “males to train or practice with an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls” [1] if no female loses a place, opportunity, scholarship, admission or other sports benefit. Shared training remains a way to work together across differences.
arguments.con_html:
Response Accepting girls who object to a matchup is different from accepting their rule for who else may compete.

  • Because The complaint explains the school’s religious objection to playing that game: “it would be affirming that sex is mutable, in violation of its beliefs.” [5] Mutable means able to change. That explains the objection. It does not make meeting the school’s demand an act of accepting people across differences.
  • Because Accepting people despite disagreement does not mean adopting their demands about others. The UNESCO declaration on tolerance, an international statement, makes this clear: “It means that one is free to adhere to one's own convictions and accepts that others adhere to theirs.” [6]
  • Because H.R.28 would make it unlawful for federally funded programs to allow “a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.” [1] The same rule would apply across covered programs, whether or not anyone objects. Its definition rests on “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1]
  • So The forfeit explains why the school wants a different rule for who may compete. It does not show why respecting these girls gives [NAME] a tolerance-based reason to impose that rule on other participants.
  • Because The training exception begins: “Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to prohibit” [1]. It leaves shared training possible under stated conditions. It does not require any cooperation across differences.
  • So Permission to train together does not supply the missing link between enforcing the objection and accepting people despite disagreement.

Even shared training is allowed only “so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot on a team or sport, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1], among other protected benefits. A roster spot is a place on a team.
  • Because Girls’ teams can offer a setting for learning to work with different people. A player in a study of two high school teams with players of many ethnic backgrounds described her own learning: “I’m learning—I learn from my team—cooperation, tolerance, and patience.” [7]

arguments.title: It replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.

Point 1 It replaces acceptance of transgender teammates with exclusion required by law.

  • Because On January 14, 2025, Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, protected participation in at least some cases. In a 2024 case, “The Fourth Circuit ruled that application of the West Virginia law to the plaintiff violated Title IX, because it treated her worse than those similarly situated based on her sex and caused her harm.” [8] The Fourth Circuit is a federal appeals court. Similarly situated means in a comparable position.
  • Because Differences between individuals mattered to that ruling. The court criticized a ban that applied “regardless of whether a particular student has any genuine athletic advantages” [8]. H.R.28 would instead make birth biology and genetics decide the question for every student it classifies as male.
  • Because [NAME] values accepting people even when they disagree. That gives weight to including a classmate despite disagreement about that classmate’s gender, and to hearing the student’s situation before ruling the student out.
  • So The bill would close a path to acceptance that the law then in force protected. Hearing individual students, or choosing inclusion as a school community, could no longer change eligibility under its birth-based rule.
  • Because The restriction also reaches activities tied to team membership. The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • Because Shared sports offer chances to know people. Researchers describe “regular social interaction; opportunities to build positive relationships with teammates and coaches” [9].
  • Because Exclusion also marks students as outsiders. The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights warns that “denying transgender, nonbinary, and intersex youth the chance to participate only serves to deny them an opportunity to be part of that community, further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10] Stigma means shame or disapproval attached to a group.
  • Note The limited permission for “males to train or practice” [1] does not give back eligibility to compete on girls’ and women’s teams.
  • So Required exclusion takes away shared competition and team-linked chances to build understanding, while adding to stigma against these classmates. [NAME]’s wish to accept and understand different people gives a reason to keep those chances and resist that treatment.
arguments.con_html:

  • Because Accepting people across disagreements leaves room to disagree about rules. [NAME] can listen to a student, understand the student’s situation and accept the student while reaching a different view about team eligibility. The research defining this value says it concerns “accepting and understanding those with life-styles and beliefs different from one’s own.” [11]
  • Because The bill sets a rule for sports eligibility: “For the purposes of this subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] A decision under that rule does not show how classmates regard or listen to the student.
  • So Treating eligibility itself as acceptance assumes the point in question. This response does not answer the claims that exclusion reduces contact and team-linked chances to build understanding, adds stigma, or removes a school’s choice to include.

  • Because Rules based on hormones allowed these matchups in U.S. college sports. Testosterone is a hormone.   • Because World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, links size and speed differences to injury: “When two opponents in a tackle are significantly different with respects to mass or speed, these risk factors increase significantly.” [6] This passage is about risks of head and neck injury. A tackle is when one player stops another by force.
  • Because Its review of lowering testosterone concluded that “safety and fairness cannot presently be assured for women competing against transwomen in contact rugby.” [7]

arguments.title: It protects girls’ chances to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 It protects girls’ chances to gain physical and mental health benefits from sports.

  • Because Limited team places can mean lost participation. ABC7 News reported that Taylor Starling was moved to the junior varsity (lower) team when a transgender runner joined a seven-place varsity (top) team, “causing Starling to miss a varsity cross-country meet.” [14] After a complaint under Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, she “was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet.” [14]
  • Because The bill keeps female competition for those female at birth. It also makes male practice depend on protecting each female’s “opportunity to participate in a practice or competition” [1].
  • So The bill prevents that source of exclusion from female competition and practice. Where a girl has no other team place, this keeps her chance to exercise on a team open.
  • Because The federal health department explains that sports “participation is one way for youth to get the physical activity they need to be fit and healthy.” [15]
  • Because A U.S. study compared girls with boys during Title IX’s expansion of girls’ sports. It reported that the expansion “resulted in greater physical activity and improved weight and body mass.” [16]
  • Because The CDC, the federal public-health agency, states that “regular physical activity prevents risk factors for various health conditions like heart disease, obesity, and type 2 diabetes.” [17]
  • Because The CDC also reports that active young people have “stronger bones and muscles.” [17] The brain-health benefits it lists include “reduced symptoms of depression.” [17]
  • So Keeping sports opportunities open protects a way to get exercise and its physical and mental health benefits. Protecting that way serves [NAME]’s wish to protect health and avoid disease.
arguments.con_html:
Response The one team-place example given does not show lost access to healthy exercise.

  • Because Starling “was bumped down to the JV team.” [14] JV means junior varsity.
  • Because The report adds that “she was moved back up to the varsity cross-country team, only missing that one meet. ML remains on the team as well.” [14]
  • So Starling kept access to school sports, and both runners ended up on the varsity team. Losing varsity status for one meet does not show less exercise or lost health benefits.
  • Because The health study concerns more girls joining sports: “Title IX caused a significant increase in girls’ sports participation.” [16]
  • So That research is about girls added to sports, while the example is about a girl who stayed active. The evidence given does not support the step from being moved down to exercising less. This response does not address a girl cut from a team with limited places and no other place to play.

  • Because The bill sets a birth-sex rule but does not say how to check it. Representative Hayes noted that it provides “neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources” [18].
  • Because Idaho passed an intrusive rule for checking sex. The Ninth Circuit, a federal appeals court, described it as allowing “intrusive medical procedures to verify her sex, including gynecological exams” [19]. A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs.
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that H.R.28 invites “invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [9] that “make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [9].
  • Because Such checks also threaten mental health. The court explained: “The psychological burden of these searches falls not only on transgender women like Lindsay but also on all women and girls who play female athletics.” [19]
  • Because Fear of checks also threatens participation. Representative Randall warned that intrusive questions and examinations would be “dissuading girls' participation in sports” [9]. Dissuading means persuading people not to do something.
  • So The new federal eligibility rule creates risks of bodily intrusion, abuse and distress in an ordinary school activity. By discouraging girls from playing, it also threatens the health benefits of exercise. Avoiding these dangers serves [NAME]’s aim to stay safe and healthy.
arguments.con_html:
Response Idaho’s separate medical-testing rule does not establish that H.R.28 would expose girls to intrusive exams.

  • Because H.R.28 defines sex by “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without ordering medical inspections. The House member managing the bill described the intended method: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [9]
  • Because The Idaho court tied intrusive checks to that state’s separate “sex dispute verification provision” [19]. It also reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [19]
  • So The argument’s own court source gives a working alternative to intrusive exams under comparable restrictions. Idaho shows that a legislature can choose exams, but it does not show that schools under H.R.28 would choose them over records. The claims of exam-related abuse and trauma depend on that step. This response does not address questions based on records, or fear and withdrawal caused by the possibility of challenges.

The same court reported that most states with categorical bans verified sex through a birth certificate. H.R.28 specifies no verification process. Sources: [19], [1].

It describes the underlying science of retained advantage as subject to ongoing debate. A word search of the full opinion text found no discussion of sex-verification procedures or examinations. arguments.pro_html:
Point 3 Exclusion cuts access to sports as a way to build safer communities.

  • Because Requiring transgender students to play on teams based on sex at birth drives some out of sports. A 2025 study summarizes earlier research: “policies requiring youth to play on teams with their assigned sex, dissuade youth from participating” [16]. To dissuade means to persuade people not to do something.
  • Because The loss also reaches girls born with variations in sex traits, often called intersex variations. Women’s sports organizations report: “Similar bans have been widely used to push girls and women born with these variations out of sports opportunities and have chilled their participation in school sports.” [10] Chilled means made people afraid to take part.
  • Note The conditional practice exception allows “males to train or practice” [1]. It guarantees no place in practice and leaves the competition ban in place.
  • So Where schools now include them, the bill cuts off a way into sports for students it excludes or discourages.
  • Because Sports also provide a setting linked to less use of illegal drugs. A review of 17 studies that followed young people over time reports: “Sport participation was associated with reduced illicit drug use during adolescence.” [17] Associated means the two happen together. It does not by itself prove cause.
  • Because The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) describes organized sports as a tool for preventing violence: “Research shows that organized sport participation can reduce youth violence” [18].
  • Because School sports build community ties. The civil rights coalition explains that “School athletics are very often the centerpiece of communities across the country” [10] and that exclusion means “further isolating and stigmatizing these youth.” [10] HHS links sports with “Improved teamwork, social skills, and social responsibility” [19].
  • Because Community ties are connected with public safety. The U.S. Surgeon General, a top federal health official, links stronger community ties with “lower levels of community violence” [20].
  • So Exclusion closes a way to cooperation, community ties, less illegal drug use and, as HHS describes it, violence prevention. Keeping those forms of protection helps the United States protect its people. That serves [NAME]’s goal of a secure, stable country.

Sports-based Programmes and Reducing Youth Violence and Crime.” [18] That review states: “None of the evaluations present robust enough evidence to directly establish causal links between interventions and outcomes.” [21] It reports some correlational evidence, meaning things that happen together, not proof of cause.
  • Because A separate review of studies on youth crime concludes that “in general, sports involvement is not reliably related to more or less juvenile delinquency” [22]. Delinquency means youth crime. HHS itself says: “Coaching, program design, and funding affect these outcomes” [18].
  • So Fewer sports places cannot simply stand for lost crime prevention. The argument has not linked the affected programs to the features that provide that protection.
  • Because The Surgeon General’s discussion of lower crime concerns residents’ “willingness to act” [20] for community members.
  • So Losing a school sports tie and losing trust in a neighborhood are different outcomes, and the argument does not connect them. This response does not address the drug-use route.

arguments.title: The bill takes a decision about children’s upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 2 The bill takes a decision about children’s upbringing away from families and local groups already responsible for it.

  • Because The Southern Baptist Convention, a large Christian denomination, teaches that “parents are the primary stewards of and decision-makers for their children, rather than teachers, doctors, or the state” [18]. A steward is someone responsible for caring for something.
  • Because Catholic teaching protects work that smaller groups can do themselves. It calls it an injustice to “assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do.” [19]
  • Because Sports rules are already partly a local responsibility: “Currently, schools, parents, and communities manage youth sports leagues and write rules about who can participate in different sports at different levels.” [14]
  • Because Existing reviews of individual students already consider safety and fairness. The Congressional Research Service describes Illinois’s 2024–25 rules as “requiring approval to participate based on consideration of individual circumstances” [6] and as considering whether “allowing eligibility would be inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • Because H.R.28 would remove that choice at covered schools. As Representative Norcross explained: “It inflicts blanket bans without the ability of states, local governments, schools, and parents to make reasonable exceptions.” [20]
  • So Even when parents and a willing school approve a child’s participation after an individual review, the federal rule would bar girls’ competition if it classifies that child as male. Keeping the family and local roles taught by [NAME]’s tradition gives a reason to oppose that loss of authority.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument has not shown that the particular sports exception being removed belongs to the family and local duties its religious sources protect.

  • Because The cited Baptist resolution places parents’ decisions “under the authority of God, recognizing that they will be held responsible for their choices” [18].
  • Because The Ethics & Religious Liberty Commission, a Southern Baptist agency, explains: “The duty of parental authority is not the right to teach children whatever they desire. Rather, it is normed by what is good, true, and righteous.” [21] Normed by means limited by that standard.
  • Because That same body addressed this sports decision on January 13, 2025: “Schools that allow biological males to participate in female sports programs are discriminating against biological females.” [22]
  • So In this account, approval by parents and a school does not turn that eligibility exception into an act of Christian care or rightful parental teaching. The argument cannot conclude that religious authority protects the exception just because parents and a school want it.
  • Because The Catholic principle of leaving work to smaller groups also serves duties beyond those groups. The same source says: “To ensure the common good, the government of each country has the specific duty to harmonize the different sectoral interests with the requirements of justice” [19]. Harmonize means bring together.
  • Because Illinois’s 2024–25 policy made eligibility a decision for the statewide sports association: “IHSA will make final rulings on student participation.” [23] Its review considered whether eligibility would be “inconsistent with concepts of fairness in competition or present a risk of injury to the participants” [6].
  • So Showing that a lower body can run a review does not show that its eligibility standard meets the religious account of justice. The argument has not shown that allowing this exception is a duty the cited traditions reserve to families or local groups. Its claim of lost religious authority therefore lacks the needed link.

Point 3 Disputes over sex eligibility can conflict with religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy.

Representative Hayes says: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [24]
  • Because Women’s sports organizations warn that resulting checks “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [14].
  • Because Questions about intimate matters have occurred under a comparable state ban. The National Women’s Law Center reports that a Florida investigation included “interviews with her teammates on if they saw her undressed.” [25]
  • Because Catholic teaching connects children’s privacy to moral upbringing: “Respect for privacy must be considered in close connection with decency and modesty” [26]. Modesty is keeping the body and private matters covered or private.
  • So Applying the rule in schools that now allow participation would require them to settle disputes about sex eligibility. The Florida account documents intimate questions, and the organizations also warn of invasive checks. For [NAME], keeping the particular religious practices of modesty and intimate privacy supplies the Tradition connection. General safety and dignity are separate reasons.
arguments.con_html:
Response The House member managing the bill identifies a way to use records, which limits the argument about bodily examinations.

original_mapping.title: It gives the United States an enforceable, lasting safeguard against injury risks from physical mismatches in women’s contact competition.
original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 1 It gives the United States an enforceable, lasting safeguard against injury risks from physical mismatches in women’s contact competition.

  • Because Title IX, the federal law against sex discrimination in education, had no express rule for transgender athletes: “Neither the statute nor the regulations currently address how Title IX applies to transgender athletes.” [3] A statute is a law. Regulations are rules written by a government agency.
  • Because May 2024 rules of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, allowed transgender women to qualify for women’s rugby through a limit on testosterone, a hormone. Transgender women are people classified male at birth who identify as women. The rules state: “Total serum testosterone thresholds apply to any transgender woman competing on an NCAA women’s team.” [4] The rugby line sets its blood testosterone limit at “<10 nmol/L” [4], meaning below that level.
  • Because A 2021 review of studies of transgender women who were not athletes found evidence of strength retained after hormone treatment: “transwomen likely retain a strength advantage over cisgender women.” [5] Cisgender women are women whose gender identity matches their sex at birth.
  • Because World Rugby, the international body for the contact sport of rugby, explains how size and speed differences affect injury risk in tackles: “the discrepancy in mass and speed of direct opponents in tackles predicts neck forces, moments and head accelerations.” [6] It adds: “Since these factors contribute directly to injury risk, it is clear that large discrepancies create greater risks for smaller and slower players, particularly when size and speed exist in combination.” [6] A discrepancy is a difference.
  • Because World Rugby’s review connects advantages kept after hormone treatment to that risk: “The lowering of testosterone removes only a small proportion of the documented biological differences, with large, retained advantages in these physiological attributes, with the safety and performance implications described previously.” [6]
  • So In covered women’s rugby, the bill would exclude competitors who went through male puberty and keep those advantages. That removes this source of risk in competition, rather than relying on a testosterone limit to remove it.
  • Because Title IX already has ways to enforce the new duty: “Title IX is primarily enforced in two ways: through private litigation in federal court and by federal agencies that distribute funding to education programs.” [3] Private litigation means lawsuits brought by people or groups.
  • So Making that participation an express Title IX violation gives federal agencies and affected students a legal basis to demand that covered schools follow the rule. This includes places where state rules allow the participation.
  • So Writing the eligibility test into the law also prevents a future president’s administration from reversing that duty simply by changing how an agency reads Title IX.
  • Note The January 2025 ruling had already removed the 2024 Title IX regulations: “a federal district court vacated them in January 2025.” [3] Vacated means canceled. Removing those regulations did not create the bill’s express national eligibility duty.
  • So Enforceable, lasting protection against this physical risk strengthens the country’s ability to defend its citizens through federal institutions. That serves [NAME]’s wish for a strong U.S. state that protects citizens against threats.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response Making protection from rugby injuries a lasting federal duty does not establish the gain in societal security this argument claims.

  • Because This value separates society’s safety from personal safety: “Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety.” [7]
  • Because World Rugby’s injury argument is about impacts on players’ bodies: “the discrepancy in mass and speed of direct opponents in tackles predicts neck forces, moments and head accelerations.” [6]
  • So That evidence is about players’ safety. It does not show how the risk threatens the country’s security or stability.
  • Because The ways to enforce the law already exist: “Title IX is primarily enforced in two ways: through private litigation in federal court and by federal agencies that distribute funding to education programs.” [3]
  • So A new eligibility duty changes what those institutions enforce. Its national reach and protection from reversal do not show that those institutions become better able to meet threats to society.
  • So The argument needs a link from this sports protection to a safer, more stable country or a stronger state able to defend its citizens. Federal enforcement and a lasting rule do not supply that link.

original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 1 The birth-sex rule creates pressure for invasive checks that expose girls to sexual abuse.

  • Because Schools must meet the new rule without a clear way to check sex. Representative Hayes explains: “H.R. 28 provides neither a specific enforcement mechanism nor resources to ensure that students participating in athletics meet these new standards.” [11]
  • Because Another birth-sex sports ban shows the enforcement risk. In 2024, a federal appeals court described Idaho’s law as allowing sex challenges and checks “including gynecological exams.” [12] A gynecological exam is a medical exam of female sex organs.
  • Because The National Women’s Law Center and Women’s Sports Foundation warn that checks under H.R.28 “may include forcing women and girls to submit to a variety of invasive, humiliating, and unscientific practices” [10]. They name the danger: “These procedures make all women and girls vulnerable to sexual abuse” [10].
  • Note The House member managing the bill proposes checking “a person's birth certificate.” [10] The bill does not make that document the final answer. Its test remains “reproductive biology and genetics at birth.” [1] That assurance does not prevent schools from adopting invasive checks.
  • So Creating a risk of abuse in schools weakens the state’s protection of its citizens. [NAME]’s commitment to a strong state that can defend them gives a reason to oppose this rule.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response The evidence does not show that H.R.28 would push schools toward invasive checks and more exposure to sexual abuse, or how such a risk would weaken societal security.

  • Because Idaho added a specific rule for medical checks: “A dispute regarding a student’s sex shall be resolved by the school or institution by requesting that the student provide a health examination and consent form or other statement signed by the student’s personal health care provider that shall verify the student’s biological sex.” [12]
  • Because The same court reported: “Most states that have instituted categorical bans on transgender participation in student athletics have verified sex via a student’s birth certificate.” [12] It also said that, among the other 24 states with restrictions, “none has authorized a similar sex verification process.” [12]
  • Because H.R.28 defines sex through “a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth” [1] without adding Idaho’s procedure for medical checks. The House member managing the bill proposed using records: “There is no requirement for inspections, and there is no necessary effort other than going to a person's birth certificate.” [10]
  • So Idaho’s added procedure explains the risk of invasive checks in that example. The wider comparison shows an established way to check sex through records. The argument does not show why H.R.28’s definition, or its failure to make birth certificates final, would replace that approach. Its warning therefore does not establish the added pressure its abuse claim needs.
  • Because This value also separates society’s safety from personal safety: “Societal security values concern safety and stability in the wider society rather than personal safety.” [7]
  • So Even if some girls faced this risk, the argument would still need to show how it weakens the country’s stability or the state’s ability to protect its people. Saying that a school harm weakens state protection does not supply that link.

original_mapping.title: It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.
original_mapping.pro_html:
Point 4 It protects religious customs of bodily privacy by ending access to intimate team activities gained through a place as a female competitor.

  • Because Southern Baptists, a large Christian denomination, defend “the privacy concerns women rightly have about sharing sleeping quarters and intimate facilities with members of the opposite sex” [12]. Intimate facilities are places for changing clothes or washing.
  • Because Competition can bring access to changing areas. The 2024 manual for a women’s swimming championship of the NCAA, the main college sports organization, provides “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. It connects athlete access to credentials, which are passes: “Team staff will receive numbered wristbands and student-athletes will receive labeled credentials. No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13]
  • Because Such access has been reported. Representative Walberg quoted swimmer Riley Gaines: “that man walked into the women's locker room at your university and saw me undress down to full nudity.” [14]
  • Because The bill covers activities beyond the contest itself, including “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1]
  • So A male athlete excluded from female competition cannot gain access to its private team activities through a place as a female competitor. Removing that way into shared intimate facilities supports the religious custom of privacy between the sexes that [NAME] wants to uphold.
original_mapping.con_html:
Response The argument does not establish that a place in female competition itself gives shared intimate access, that the bill covers those facilities, or that the cited statement describes an inherited custom.

  • Because The swimming manual describes “locker rooms dedicated to the users of the competition pool” [13]. That passage does not say which users may use which room, or that those rooms are shared across sexes.
  • Because Its credential rule says: “No one will be allowed to enter the facility or access the pool deck without proper identification.” [13] This makes identification necessary to enter the building. It does not make a competition pass permission to change or shower with women.
  • Because The bill includes “all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team.” [1] Applying that clause to the claimed intimate access requires evidence that the access is a benefit that depends on team participation. The manual does not establish that condition for sharing intimate facilities with women.
  • So The legal path to these facilities is not established.
  • Because The Baptist resolution lists “the privacy concerns women rightly have” [12] among its reasons to oppose a civil-rights bill. It does not describe an inherited custom or ask people to keep one because of continuity with the past.
  • So Religious support for a privacy concern does not by itself establish a Tradition reason. This response does not address the separate point that a person excluded from female competition would no longer have that competition as a reason to use its changing area.
